passages.t: A poor widow's two small coins
passages.happening:
Jesus looks up and sees rich people putting their gifts into the temple treasury. He also sees “a poor widow put in two small copper coins” (verse 2).

“Truly I tell you,” he says, “this poor widow has put in more than all the others. For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on” (verses 3-4).
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story too (Mark 12:41-44), and the note there explains the scene. Her two coins were the smallest coins in use in that land. Two of them made a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin, and it took sixty-four of those to make one denarius, a day's wage. Her gift was worth a few minutes of a labourer's work.

A widow was often among the poorest people in the land, with no husband to provide for her and no one to defend her rights. Notice what comes just before. Jesus has warned about scribes who “defraud widows of their houses” (20:47). Now a widow gives everything she has. And just after, Jesus will say that the temple she gave to will be thrown down (21:6). Luke sets the three side by side.
passages.ot:
Widows were God's special concern in the Law: “You must not mistreat any widow or orphan” (Exodus 22:22). God is called “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows” (Psalm 68:5).

The Old Testament also knew that God looks at the heart, not the size: “man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).
passages.hard:
Does Jesus praise the widow, or grieve over what was done to her? Most readers through the centuries have heard praise. Jesus says she gave more than all the rest, because she gave everything. Her gift points ahead to Jesus himself, who will soon give his whole life.

In 1982 the scholar Addison Wright argued for another reading. The story comes right after Jesus condemns those who devour widows' houses, and right before he says the temple will be torn down. Jesus never says she did well or tells anyone to copy her. So, Wright argued, Jesus is lamenting that a system had taught a poor woman to give her last coins to a temple about to fall. Others have answered that this reading is clever but misses the plain tone. Many readers now hold both: Jesus honours her real and costly devotion, and he condemns leaders who should have been caring for her instead of taking from her.

What the story does not teach is that the poor must give away what they need to live, or that God's favour can be bought.
passages.asks: God measures a gift by what it costs, not by its size. Ask what you give God from your leftovers, and whether there is anything you give that truly costs you. And if you are a leader, ask whether anyone in your care is giving out of need while you look away.

passages.t: Not one stone left: do not be deceived, do not be alarmed
passages.happening:
Some of the disciples are talking about how the temple is adorned with beautiful stones and with gifts given to God. Jesus says, “the time will come when not one stone will be left on another; every one will be thrown down” (verse 6).

They ask him when this will happen, and what sign will show it is about to take place. Jesus answers, “See to it that you are not deceived.” Many will come in his name, saying ‘I am He’ and ‘The time is near.’ “Do not follow them” (verse 8). “When you hear of wars and rebellions, do not be alarmed. These things must happen first, but the end is not imminent” (verse 9). Nation will rise against nation. There will be earthquakes, famines and diseases, “along with fearful sights and great signs from heaven” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew both give this teaching, and the notes on Mark 13 and Matthew 24 explain it. Luke's form has its own shape. In Mark the disciples ask their question on the Mount of Olives. In Luke Jesus is still in the temple, teaching, and the people can hear.

The disciple who admired the stones was not wrong to be impressed. Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 or 19 BC, and work on the courts went on for decades after his death. Josephus, who saw it, wrote that from a distance it looked like a mountain covered with snow, and that parts of it were covered with gold. He also tells of the spoils of war that Herod dedicated and fixed around the temple, and of a great golden vine with hanging clusters. The ‘gifts’ the disciples admired were offerings of this kind.

Within about forty years it was gone. The Jewish revolt against Rome began in AD 66. In AD 70 a Roman army under Titus took Jerusalem, and the temple burned.

Only Luke has the false teachers say, ‘The time is near.’ Jesus warns his followers against exactly that kind of preacher, the one who announces that the end has come.
passages.ot: Jesus was not the first Jew to say the temple would fall. Centuries earlier the prophet Micah had said, “Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble” (Micah 3:12), and Jeremiah warned the people not to trust in the building as if it made them safe (Jeremiah 7:4). The first temple, built by Solomon, was destroyed by Babylon. Jesus speaks in the line of those prophets. He speaks from inside Israel, with grief, and not as an enemy.
passages.hard:
Every age has had wars, earthquakes, and famines, and in every age someone has said they prove the end is here. Jesus says the opposite. These things must happen first, “but the end is not imminent”. They are not a countdown. They are the normal weather of a broken world, and Jesus tells his followers not to be alarmed by them.

If the news frightens you, or you were taught as a child to dread the end of the world, notice the first thing Jesus says after the wars: ‘do not be alarmed’. He does not hand his followers a chart to watch. These notes offer no end-times timetable, and no date.
passages.asks: The first danger Jesus names is not war. It is being fooled. Ask who you let tell you what the news means, and whether fear makes you easier to fool. Be slow to trust anyone who tells you ‘The time is near’ and asks you to follow him.

passages.t: Before kings and governors: not a hair of your head
passages.happening:
“But before all this,” Jesus says, “they will seize you and persecute you” (verse 12). His followers will be handed over to synagogues and prisons, and brought before kings and governors because of his name. “This will be your opportunity to serve as witnesses” (verse 13).

They are not to worry beforehand about how to defend themselves. “For I will give you speech and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict” (verse 15). They will be betrayed even by parents, brothers, relatives and friends, and some will be put to death. “And you will be hated by everyone because of My name. Yet not even a hair of your head will perish. By your patient endurance you will gain your souls” (verses 17-19).
passages.hearers:
Luke wrote a second book, Acts, and in it these words come true one after another. Peter and John are seized and brought before the council in Jerusalem (Acts 4). Stephen's opponents “could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke” (Acts 6:10), and he is killed. Paul is held in prison and brought before the Roman governors Felix and Festus and before King Agrippa (Acts 24 to 26). Luke's first readers would have recognised their own story here.

In Mark, Jesus says the Holy Spirit will speak through them (Mark 13:11). In Luke, Jesus says ‘I will give you speech and wisdom’. Luke has already said the Spirit will teach them what to say (12:12). For Luke, the risen Jesus and his Spirit work as one.

The word ‘witnesses’ matters to Luke. At the very end of the book Jesus will say, “You are witnesses of these things” (24:48).
passages.ot:
The Psalms knew the pain of being betrayed by a friend: “Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9).

Daniel and his friends were brought before a king because they would not bow to anyone but God, and they answered him plainly (Daniel 3:16-18). Jesus' followers stand in that line.
passages.hard:
How can Jesus say ‘some of you will be put to death’ and then ‘not even a hair of your head will perish’? Readers take it in a few ways. Many read it as a promise about the whole person before God: those who belong to Jesus may lose their lives, but they will not be lost. Nothing done to them can destroy what God keeps. Others read it as a promise of the resurrection, when God will raise them whole. Jesus had already said, “even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not be afraid” (12:7). Both readings agree that it is not a promise of safety from harm.

Verse 16 speaks of family members betraying each other. That is a painful verse for anyone who has been hurt by their own family, whether for their faith or for some other reason. Jesus names that pain honestly. He does not call it good. He promises that those who endure it are not forgotten. If you are in danger, contact the police or a crisis line.
passages.asks: Jesus says that being dragged before the powerful will be a chance to speak about him. Ask where a hard place in your life might become a place to bear witness. And notice his word for how to get through: patient endurance. Not a burst of courage. Staying the course, one day at a time.

passages.t: Jerusalem surrounded by armies, and the times of the Gentiles
passages.happening:
“But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near” (verse 20). Then those in Judea must flee to the mountains, those in the city must get out, and those in the country must not go in. “For these are the days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written” (verse 22).

“How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers!” (verse 23). There will be great distress in the land. People will fall by the sword and be led away captive to all the nations. “And Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Here Luke's form is most his own. Mark and Matthew speak of ‘the abomination of desolation’, a phrase from Daniel (see the note on Mark 13:14-23). Luke says plainly, ‘Jerusalem surrounded by armies’. In AD 70 that is what happened. Josephus counts ninety-seven thousand people taken captive in the whole war.

Most scholars date Luke after AD 70, and many think these words read like someone who knew how the siege went. Others answer that siege language was common in Israel's prophets, so these words need no hindsight (see the book page, ‘When it was written’). Careful readers hold each view.

The church historian Eusebius, writing in the 300s, tells that the Christians of Jerusalem were warned before the war and left the city for Pella, a town east of the Jordan. Whether that happened is debated, because the reports come long after the events.

Notice again where Jesus' eye goes. In the middle of a city's ruin he thinks of pregnant women and nursing mothers.
passages.ot:
‘All that is written’ points back to the prophets' warnings over Jerusalem. Jeremiah cried, “flee from Jerusalem!” (Jeremiah 6:1), before the Babylonians took the city. Moses had warned that God says, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32:35), and Hosea said, “The days of punishment have come” (Hosea 9:7). These are words spoken by Israel's own prophets, inside Israel's story.

The Old Testament also knew of foreign nations trampling the holy city for a time, and of God setting a limit to it (Daniel 8:13-14).
passages.hard:
Does ‘wrath against this people’ mean God has cast off the Jewish people? No. Christians have quoted this verse with contempt, and that was wrong. These are the words of a Jewish prophet, weeping over his own city, in the line of Jeremiah. The judgment falls on a city in a time of war, as it had in Jeremiah's day; it is not a sentence on a people for all time. And the sentence has a limit: ‘until’.

What are ‘the times of the Gentiles’? Readers take the phrase in several ways. Some read it as the time when Jerusalem would be ruled by foreign nations, ending when God's plan for the city is complete. Some read it as the age when the good news goes out to the nations, and compare Paul's hope that Israel's hardening lasts only “until the full number of the Gentiles has come in” (Romans 11:25). Some hold that after these times God will restore Israel. Faithful Christians differ on the details, and on whether the modern state of Israel has any place in them. These notes do not choose.

Some have tried to work out the year when the times of the Gentiles end, and the years they named have come and gone. Jesus gave no year. These notes set out no end-times scheme and no date. If a teacher offers you one, remember Jesus' words: “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority” (Acts 1:7).
passages.asks: Jesus told his followers to run, not to stay and defend the holy place. Ask what you would cling to if you had to leave everything. And ask how you speak of other people's suffering. Jesus spoke of the fall of Jerusalem with tears and with care for mothers and babies, never with gloating.

passages.happening:
“There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on the earth dismay among the nations, bewildered by the roaring of the sea and the surging of the waves” (verse 25). People will faint from fear at what is coming on the world, “for the powers of the heavens will be shaken” (verse 26).

“At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (verses 27-28).
passages.hearers:
The pictures of sun, moon and stars come from Israel's prophets, who used them for the great days when God acts in judgment and rescue. The roaring sea was an old picture of chaos, the forces that God alone can calm. Luke has already shown Jesus calming a storm (8:24).

Only Luke has verse 28. Everyone else faints with fear. Jesus' followers are told to stand up and lift their heads. ‘Redemption’ means being set free, bought back. Old Anna, in the temple, spoke about the baby Jesus “to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem” (2:38). What frightens the world is, for those who trust him, the sign that their rescue is near.
passages.ot:
Isaiah said that on the day of the LORD, “the stars of heaven and their constellations will not give their light” (Isaiah 13:10). Joel said, “The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood” (Joel 2:31).

Daniel saw “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13), who was given a kingdom that would never end. Jesus takes that name for himself.
passages.hard:
Does this passage describe the end of history, or the events of AD 70?

Many Christians read these verses as the second coming of Christ at the end of the age, when he returns in glory. This has been the most common reading through the centuries. Luke's order supports a gap: the city is trodden down ‘until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled’ before these signs come.

Others read the passage as describing the fall of Jerusalem in the prophets' picture-language. In Daniel, the Son of Man comes to God, not down to earth, to receive a kingdom. Those who read it this way still believe Christ will return, and they find that promise elsewhere in the New Testament.

Still others think both are in view, the near event as a picture of the final one.

Christians who hold each of these views confess together in the creeds that Christ will come again in glory. They differ on which verses describe which event. These notes leave that question open, and they offer no end-times timetable.
passages.asks: Jesus does not tell his followers to hide when the world shakes. He tells them to stand up and lift their heads. Ask whether you think about the future mostly with fear or mostly with hope, and which one this passage invites.

passages.t: The fig tree and all the trees, and ‘this generation’
passages.happening:
Jesus tells them a parable: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they sprout leaves, you can see for yourselves and know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near” (verses 29-31).

“Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away” (verses 32-33).
passages.hearers: Many trees in the land of Israel, such as the olive, keep their leaves all year. The fig tree does not. It stands bare through winter, and when its new leaves come, summer is close. Luke adds ‘and all the trees’, perhaps for readers who lived far from Judea. Any tree will do. And where Mark says ‘He is near’, Luke says ‘the kingdom of God is near’.
passages.ot: Jesus' words echo Isaiah: “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Jesus speaks of his own words the way Isaiah spoke of God's word.
passages.hard:
Verse 32 is one of the hardest in the Bible. If ‘all these things’ includes the coming of the Son of Man, did Jesus promise that the end would come within his hearers' lifetimes? Many skeptics have said yes, and that he was wrong. The objection is serious, and Christians have felt it too. C. S. Lewis, a believer, called the same saying in Mark ‘the most embarrassing verse in the Bible’ in his essay The World's Last Night.

Christians have answered in three main ways.

One reading says that ‘all these things’ means the signs and the fall of the city, which did happen within about forty years. The coming itself follows at a time no one knows. Readers who hold this point out that in verse 31 ‘these things’ are signs seen before the kingdom is near, so they cannot include its coming.

A second reading says that the whole passage up to verse 32 describes AD 70, read in the prophets' picture-language, and was fulfilled within that generation.

A third reading takes ‘this generation’ in another sense, such as the generation that sees the signs, or even the kind of people who resist God.

Each view has a weakness its critics point to, and careful Christians hold each one. When Jesus will return is a question on which faithful Christians differ. That he will return is confessed by all.
passages.asks: Jesus stakes everything on his words. Heaven and earth will go, but what he has said will stand. Ask whose words you trust most when you are afraid: the news, your own feelings, or his. A fig tree teaches you to notice. Jesus wants his followers awake to what God is doing, not scanning the sky for a date.

passages.happening:
“But watch yourselves,” Jesus says, “or your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life” (verse 34). That day could spring on them suddenly, like a trap, and it will come on everyone on earth. “So keep watch at all times, and pray that you may have the strength to escape all that is about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man” (verse 36).

Luke closes the section. Every day Jesus teaches in the temple, and every night he goes out to the Mount of Olives. “And early in the morning all the people would come to hear Him at the temple” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke ends the teaching this way. The danger Jesus names is not mainly persecution or false teachers. It is a heavy heart. ‘Dissipation’ means wild living, the kind that leaves you dull the next morning. Drunkenness is plain. And the third is ordinary worry, the cares of life. Jesus had warned of the same thing in the parable of the sower, where the seed is choked “by the worries, riches, and pleasures of this life” (8:14). Worry and drink do the same thing in different ways. They make a person stop paying attention.

The last two verses close the frame Luke opened at 19:47-48. All week Jesus teaches in the temple by day and sleeps on the Mount of Olives at night. The people come early to hear him. In the next chapter Luke will tell how the leaders found a way to take him without the crowd.

Some later manuscripts place the story of the woman caught in adultery, usually printed in John 8, right after these verses, a setting that fits Jesus teaching in the temple by day. The story is missing from the earliest manuscripts of both Gospels.
passages.ot: The prophets warned against hearts made dull by drink: “Woe to those who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink” (Isaiah 5:11). And Proverbs says, “Anxiety weighs down the heart of a man, but a good word cheers it up” (Proverbs 12:25).
passages.hard:
What does it mean to ‘escape all that is about to happen’? Some read it of the coming fall of Jerusalem, which those who watched and fled would survive. Many read it of the whole time of trouble before the end, and of standing before the Son of Man at the judgment without shame. These notes do not choose. Either way, Jesus does not tell his followers to work out a timetable. He tells them to stay awake and to pray.

These words are not given to make anyone afraid, least of all a child lying awake at night. Watching, in Luke, means a clear head and a praying heart in an ordinary day.
passages.asks: Jesus names worry beside drunkenness. Both weigh the heart down. Ask what dulls you: drink, screens, busyness, or the low hum of worry. Then ask what ‘keep watch at all times, and pray’ would look like in your ordinary week. It may be as simple as starting the day, like the people in verse 38, by coming early to listen.
